Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively, starting with searches on the survey itself.I have a good foundation. Let me dig deeper into methodology, data access, and the survey's ecosystem (API, FRED, related programs).The methodology page returned mostly boilerplate, but I already have its key content from search results. Now I'll check the current data release details and the wider ecosystem of related datasets and secondary distribution through FRED and research usage.I have strong coverage of the publisher, authority, methodology, and distribution channels. Let me fill the remaining gaps: early history and how researchers/policy analysts use the data.# Research Report: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)

**Prepared for:** Data preservation, data librarianship, data science, and policy research audiences
**Dataset verified as of:** October 2026 (most recent release: 2026 Q2, published September 24, 2026)

---

## 1. Identification & Executive Summary

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Official title** | Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP) |
| **Program code / survey ID** | QPR (used in URLs, API paths, and file directories, e.g., `census.gov/govs/qpr/`) |
| **Publisher / steward** | U.S. Census Bureau — Governments Division / public-sector statistics programs (Employment & Benefit Statistics Branch; respondent support via Economic and Wealth Statistics directorate) |
| **Type** | Quarterly *panel* collection (a census of the largest 100 systems, not a probability sample) |
| **Coverage** | The 100 largest state & local defined-benefit public employee pension systems in the U.S. |
| **Time span** | Q1 1968 – present (one of the longest-running government finance time series in existence) |
| **Frequency / lag** | Quarterly; released ~3 months after each calendar quarter |
| **Latest observation** | Q2 2026: total cash and security holdings of **$6.55 trillion** across the 100 systems |
| **Legal authority** | Title 13, U.S.C., Sections 161 and 182; OMB clearance No. 0607-0143 |
| **Cost** | Free, public domain, no restrictions |
| **Contact** | ewd.pensions@census.gov; 1-888-529-1963 |

**Bottom line:** QSPP is a small but high-value federal economic indicator produced by the Census Bureau since 1968 at the original request of the Council of Economic Advisers and the Federal Reserve Board. It is a primary input into the Fed's Financial Accounts (Flow of Funds) and BEA's National Income and Product Accounts/GDP, and it is the nation's only timely, consistent, quarterly measure of public pension asset composition. Its published tables are **national aggregates only** — system- and state-level detail lives in the related Annual Survey of Public Pensions and the quinquennial Census of Governments.

**Verification note on your description:** Your text is accurate with two caveats. (1) The official name is the Quarterly **Survey** of Public Pensions; "Quarterly **Summary** of Public Pensions" appears in some Census "About" pages as a legacy phrasing — the survey was indeed previously titled the *Finances of Selected State and Local Government Employee Retirement Systems* and later the *Quarterly Survey of the Finances of Public Employee Retirement Systems*. (2) Although called a "survey," it is a full canvass of the 100 largest systems rather than a probability sample — important, because Census states the data "are not subject to sampling error," only to nonsampling error.

---

## 2. Publisher & Institutional Stewardship

- **Producing agency:** U.S. Census Bureau, within its public-sector (governments) statistics program. Historically housed in the Governments Division; the branch responsible is the Employment and Benefit Statistics Branch.
- **Program family:** QSPP sits in the Census Bureau's **economic indicator surveys** group (alongside the Quarterly Summary of State & Local Taxes, Quarterly Financial Report, etc.). Note that QSPP is explicitly *not* one of the "principal" federal economic indicators (like retail sales or new home sales), but is classified among the supporting economic indicator time series.
- **Topic hierarchy:** Census topic areas "Public Sector → Public Pensions → Government Employee Retirement Systems."
- **Funding:** Appropriated by Congress; the program is described by Census as part of the "Recurring Programs Area."
- **Survey clearance:** Renewed through the Paperwork Reduction Act process; the Federal Register notice cycle (e.g., a 2011 comment request) shows the OMB review history. Current OMB approval number **0607-0143**, expiring 12/31/2027.

---

## 3. Legal Authority & Mandate

- **Statutory authorization:** Title 13, United States Code, **Sections 161 and 182** authorize the Census Bureau to conduct this collection and to request respondents' assistance.
- **Voluntary participation:** Unlike the decennial census or economic census, QSPP responses are **voluntary** — Census asks for "voluntary assistance" under §182.
- **Confidentiality treatment:** The data are subject to **Title 13, U.S.C., Section 9(b)**, which exempts data "customarily provided in public records" from confidentiality rules. Public pension systems' financial reports are typically public records, so these data are not held confidential — which is why aggregate publication is unrestricted.
- **Cybersecurity:** Respondent data are protected under the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015 through screening of transmission systems.
- **Respondent obligations/dates:** Due dates are May 15 (Q1), Aug. 14 (Q2), Nov. 12 (Q3), and Feb. 11 (Q4); respondents may submit up to 8 quarters late, with late data incorporated into later revisions.

---

## 4. History & Evolution

### Origins (1968)
The quarterly collection was **initiated by the Census Bureau in 1968 at the request of both the Council of Economic Advisers and the Federal Reserve Board**, who needed timely data on the growing pool of public pension assets for national accounts and flow-of-funds purposes. (Documented in Federal Register clearance notices.)

### Name changes
- 1968–2011: *Finances of Selected State and Local Government Employee Retirement Systems* (also cited as *Quarterly Survey of the Finances of Public Employee Retirement Systems*)
- **Effective Q1 2012: renamed the Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)**, with simultaneous content improvements.

### Panel history (documented in Census user notes)
| Period | Panel size |
|---|---|
| 1969–1973 | 100 largest systems |
| 1974–1976 | 111 |
| 1977–1979 | 106 |
| 1980–1982 | 105 |
| 1983–1984 | 102 |
| 1985–1994 | 104 |
| 1995–1999 | panel size not documented |
| 2000–present | 100 |

The panel is **redrawn after each Census of Governments** (conducted every 5 years, in years ending in 2 and 7), based on total cash and security holdings. Notable redraws: the 2007 Census produced a new universe effective Q1 2009 (five systems replaced); the 2012 Census produced the current universe effective **Q1 2014** (87.2% of financial activity; an earlier FAQ cited 87.5%). A **Bridge Report** documents each panel change and its data impact — essential reading for longitudinal analysis.

### Definition/classification changes (critical for time-series work)
- **Pre-March 1978:** federal agency securities included in "other securities."
- **1978–1981:** receipt data revised for a change in nonrespondent estimation procedure.
- **March 1987:** federally sponsored agency securities reclassified into corporate bonds (1987–1989 data later re-revised into agency securities category).
- **Q4 2004:** government contributions revised to include contributions from other governments.
- **2002–Q3 2004:** earnings on investments adjusted to exclude imputed data.
- **Q1 2010:** Denver Public Schools Retirement System merged into Colorado PERA (a large one-time jump in government contributions).
- **Q1 2012 (the big one):** realized vs. unrealized net gains/losses split into separate items; federally-sponsored agency securities moved from Corporate Bonds to Federal Government Securities; **private equity, venture capital, and leveraged buyouts moved from "Other Securities" to "Corporate Stocks."**
- **September 2012:** historical QSPP data first made available in the Census Bureau's Economic Indicators database/API, dramatically improving machine access.

---

## 5. Scope, Methodology & Data Content

### Population of interest
State and local government **defined benefit** pension systems (explicitly *excluding* defined contribution plans, 401(k)-style plans, and OPEB/post-employment healthcare plans). To qualify, a system must (1) be sponsored by a Census-recognized unit of state or local government and (2) have membership comprised of public employees compensated with public funds. The frame universe is roughly **2,200 public employee retirement systems**; the surveyed panel of 100 covers about **87–89% of all financial activity** (target ≈85%).

### What is collected
- **Financial holdings (assets, end of quarter):** cash and short-term investments (checkable deposits, money market funds, time & savings deposits, reverse repos), federal government securities (Treasury, agency), corporate bonds, corporate stocks (domestic, foreign), private equity, state and local government securities, mortgages, other securities, other indirectly held assets, real property, insurance/annuity investments, and miscellaneous.
- **Revenue (during quarter):** earnings on investments (realized/unrealized gains separately since 2012), employee contributions, government contributions.
- **Expenditures (during quarter):** primarily benefit payments to retirees and beneficiaries, plus withdrawals.

### Collection mechanics
- Mail/web canvass of the 100-system panel; collection begins at the start of each calendar quarter and runs ~3 months; amounts are as of quarter-end (March, June, September, December).
- **Not subject to sampling error** (full panel canvass); subject to nonsampling errors — nonresponse, respondent error, and **imputation of nonrespondent data**.
- Response rates: usable replies from at least 80% of systems historically; recent **unit response rates of 83–99%** in 2024–25, with an early Q1 2026 estimate of 76% (total quantity response rate 82.10%) — a dip worth watching.

### Products (each quarterly release)
Three national summary tables (published ~3 months after quarter-end, showing five years of trends), plus:
- **Table: National Financial Transactions** (revenues/expenditures)
- **Table: Cash and Security Holdings of Major Public Employee Pension Systems**
- **Panel ID list** — names of the 100 systems in the current panel (fixed-length, no-delimiter text file)
- **QSPP Bridge Report** — panel-change documentation

---

## 6. Access, Formats & Distribution (Data Librarian / Preservationist View)

| Channel | Details |
|---|---|
| **Program page** | census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp (About, FAQ, methodology, user notes, respondent info) |
| **Current & historical releases** | census.gov/data/tables/time-series/econ/qspp/ — PDF and spreadsheet tables, TXT panel list, bridge report; archive at www2.census.gov/govs/qpr/ going back decades |
| **Census API** | `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr` (Economic Indicators Time Series). API key now required. Variables, groups, and examples documented at api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr.html |
| **Census trend charts** | census.gov/econ_timeseries/?programCode=QPR — interactive time-series charts back to Q1 1968 (e.g., total holdings: $38.3B in Q1 1968 → $6.55T in Q2 2026) |
| **FRED (St. Louis Fed)** | Full secondary distribution: dozens of series (release ID 450), e.g., `QPRHLDTOTTOTHOLDINGSUSNO` (Total Cash and Security Holdings, Q1 1968–present, millions of dollars, NSA). Units: not seasonally adjusted. Citation format provided |
| **ALFRED** | Archival FRED — preserves **vintage/as-first-released data** with release dates from 2019-04-25 onward; invaluable for studying revisions and real-time analysis |
| **data.census.gov** | Not the primary portal for QSPP (which predates it), but the related annual/CoG public pension datasets live there and in the `timeseries/govspension` API |

**Preservation notes:** The 1968+ quarterly time series is one of the few federal series with 55+ years of consistent quarterly coverage of a financial market segment. The fixed-length TXT panel list and PDF releases are the archival formats of record; the API only covers the modernized series. Classification breaks (especially 2012) and panel redraws mean raw concatenation of historical files without the user notes and bridge reports will produce spurious level shifts.

---

## 7. Data Quality & Limitations (Data Scientist View)

1. **No sampling error, but nonsampling error is real:** nonresponse imputation, respondent error, timing differences. Total quantity response rates (the share of total dollars accounted for by respondents) are the better quality metric and run ~87–99%.
2. **Panel breaks:** universe redrawn after each Census of Governments (currently based on the 2012 CoG). Always read the Bridge Report before long-horizon analysis.
3. **Classification breaks:** at minimum 1978, 1987, 2002, 2004, 2010 (merger), and 2012. The 2012 reclassification of private equity/VC/LBOs into corporate stocks is a level break in asset composition.
4. **Revisions:** late responses are accepted for up to 8 quarters and published in subsequent quarterly revisions — use vintages (ALFRED) if first-print values matter.
5. **Coverage gap:** ~11–13% of DB pension financial activity (and all DC plans and OPEB) are excluded. For the full universe, use the Annual Survey of Public Pensions (state- and system-level, fiscal-year, market-value assets) or the Census of Governments: Public Pensions.
6. **Geographic resolution:** published QSPP tables are **national aggregates only** — no state or system identifiers in the published data.
7. **Not seasonally adjusted** — FRED carries the series NSA; seasonality in contributions/withdrawals is left to the user.
8. **Voluntary response** — the 2025–26 response-rate softening (low-80s/upper-70s unit response) is worth monitoring for imputation-related noise.

**Handy sanity anchors:** total holdings were $2.81T at 2008 Q2 and $2.23T at 2008 Q4 (Great Recession drawdown ≈ –21% in two quarters); $6.55T as of 2026 Q2.

---

## 8. Users & Uses (Policy / Research View)

### Primary federal users (the survey's raison d'être)
- **Federal Reserve Board — the primary user.** QSPP feeds the quarterly **Financial Accounts of the United States (Flow of Funds)**, including Table L.120.b on state & local DB pension plans. The Fed's Enhanced Financial Accounts state-level pension funding visualizations are benchmarked to Census pension data.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis** — uses the data (historically the corporate-stock holdings, to estimate dividends received by governments) to update the government sector of the **National Income and Product Accounts / GDP**.
- **Council of Economic Advisers** — original 1968 requester; macro-monitoring use.

### Other documented users
- **Investment bankers and financial analysts** — tracking investment-pattern shifts of public pension systems, "among the largest types of institutional investors in the U.S. financial markets."
- **Economists and public policy specialists** — econometric models of general economic conditions and state/local fiscal activity; pension funding adequacy debates (an issue of perennial national importance given multi-trillion-dollar liabilities).
- **Journalists and think tanks** (Pew, Brookings, NCPERS-type industry trackers) as the timeliest official figure on aggregate public pension assets.
- **Academic researchers** — long quarterly series enables studies of institutional investor behavior across market cycles.

### Public benefits
- **Feeds core national statistics** (GDP, Financial Accounts) that inform monetary and fiscal policy.
- **Transparency** on how ~$6.5 trillion of public-employee retirement assets (workers' deferred compensation) are invested — publicly available, free, timely, and vendor-neutral.
- **Historical continuity** — an unbroken quarterly record since 1968 spanning seven recessions, enabling rare long-run analysis of a major institutional investor class.
- **Accountability infrastructure** — gives the public, unions, retirees, and taxpayers an official benchmark against which state-reported figures can be compared.

---

## 9. Related & Complementary Datasets

| Dataset | Relationship |
|---|---|
| **Annual Survey of Public Pensions (APRS)** | Annual, fiscal-year, **state- and system-level** detail (revenue, expenditure, assets, membership) for the full DB universe; API: `timeseries/govspension` (2012–2025) |
| **Census of Governments: Public Pensions** | Quinquennial benchmark census (years ending 2 and 7); source of the QSPP panel universe |
| **Annual Survey of State & Local Government Finances** | Broader state/local fiscal context; API: `timeseries/govsorg`-family |
| **Fed Financial Accounts (Z.1) & Enhanced Financial Accounts** | Downstream consumer of QSPP/APRS data; state-level funding-status tables |
| **FRED release 450** | Secondary distribution of all QSPP series |

---

## 10. Key References

- Program page: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp.html
- About/authority: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/about.html
- Methodology: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/methodology.html
- User notes (panel & classification history): https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/user-notes.html
- FAQ: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/about/faq.html
- Current release: https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/econ/qspp/current-release.html
- API: https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr.html
- FRED release: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=450 | ALFRED: https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=450
- Federal Register (2011 clearance, origin history): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2011/08/26/2011-21875/
- Respondent portal: https://respond.census.gov/qspp (shows OMB No. 0607-0143)

---

## 11. Summary Assessment by Audience

- **Preservationist:** High value — 58 years of quarterly continuity; preserve the PDF/TXT release archive, panel ID lists, bridge reports, and user notes alongside the API data, since reclassification documentation is essential to interpretability. ALFRED vintages (2019+) preserve revision history; earlier vintages exist only in the paper/file archive.
- **Data librarian:** Straightforward to catalog — clear publisher (Census Bureau), statutory authority (13 U.S.C. §§161, 182), OMB number (0607-0143), program code (QPR), and stable access channels (Census, FRED, API). Recommend the FRED and API copies for patrons, with links to the bridge report for methodology caveats.
- **Data scientist:** Clean, small, well-documented aggregate series; the main analytical hazards are panel breaks, 2012 classification changes, imputation during low-response quarters, and the absence of seasonal adjustment or subnational detail. Pair with the annual public pensions dataset for state-level work.
- **Policy activist:** The authoritative, timely, free national yardstick for the health and investment behavior of public pensions — the dataset behind the headline "$X trillion in public pension assets" figures, and an indirect input into GDP and the Fed's Financial Accounts. Its national-only aggregation limits system-level accountability uses; those require the APRS or Census of Governments data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The full quarterly time series (Q1 1968 – Q2 2026) remains publicly accessible: the complete archive of PDF/spreadsheet releases, panel ID lists, and bridge reports is posted at census.gov/data/tables/time-series/econ/qspp and www2.census.gov/govs/qpr; the Census API (`timeseries/eits/qpr`) and Census trend charts still serve data back to Q1 1968; and FRED/ALFRED carry every series with vintages back to April 2019 (ALFRED release-dates file, retrieved Oct. 8, 2026).
- No removals, redactions, or retroactive alterations of historical QSPP files were found in any source. Unlike ACS or small-area products, QSPP has not been named in any delay/removal action.
- The June 2026 Commerce disclosure-avoidance order (DAO 216-26) has caused indefinite delays to *other* Census products (e.g., 2025 ACS one-year estimates) but has not touched published QSPP historical tables; QSPP's published product is national aggregates of public-record financial data and does not use noise infusion.

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** All historical data remain accessible and unaltered, with multiple independent copies (Census, FRED/ALFRED).

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for High Risk (rejected):** No skipped quarter and no lapsed ICR. The ICR (OMB No. 0607-0143) was renewed December 4, 2024 as an "extension without change" and is active through 12/31/2027 (OMB.report ICR 202409-0607-003). Collection continued through 2025–2026 with published response rates every quarter.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- ALFRED vintage dates document a **missed typical release date for Q3 2025**: every prior Q3/Q4-period release came in late December (12/19/2024, 12/21/2023, 12/20/2022…), but the Q3 2025 release slipped to **January 15, 2026** — a roughly 3–4 week delay caused by the 43-day October–November 2025 government shutdown, during which most Census Bureau staff were furloughed and "collection and distribution of nearly all data" was suspended (Reuters, Oct. 21, 2025). The Bureau was still "implementing strategies to bring economic data releases back on track" in early December 2025 (Reuters/US News, Dec. 3, 2025).
- Releases have since resumed on the normal ~3-month cadence: 3/26/2026, 6/25/2026, 9/24/2026 (plus a 9/16/2026 revision) — evidence the delay was a one-time disruption, not a degraded schedule.
- ICR expiration (12/31/2027) is more than a year away, and no statutory deadline applies to QSPP.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** One missed typical publication date (shutdown-driven), but collection/publication resumed on schedule and the ICR is active — this fits "typical or intended publication date missed and/or publication delayed," not the High Risk triggers.

## Data Quality

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Frequency, granularity (same asset/revenue/expenditure detail, three summary tables, five-year trend window), and timeliness (~3-month lag) have all been maintained through the most recent release (Q2 2026, published Sept. 24, 2026). No variables have been dropped from QSPP.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- **Response rates are deteriorating.** Census's own methodology page shows unit response rates fell from 96–99% across 2024 to 83–91% across 2025, and to **76% unit response (82.10% quantity response) in Q1 2026** — the lowest in the published series, coinciding with the shutdown-disrupted collection cycle. Lower response means more imputation and greater nonsampling error in the aggregates.
- **Pending policy could reach the product.** Commerce's DAO 216-26 (June 4, 2026) bans noise infusion and mandates coarsening or suppression; the Census acting director stated it applies to "all statistical products." While QSPP publishes only national aggregates and is an unlikely candidate for suppression, implementation decisions are still undetermined (NC OSBM, Sept. 2026).
- **The sibling survey is being cut.** The August 18, 2026 Federal Register notice reveals plans to restructure the Annual Survey of Public Pensions (F-11), combining items and **dropping sixteen actuarial data items** — direct evidence of content reduction within the same pension-program family (though not QSPP itself).

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** No actual reduction in QSPP's granularity, timeliness, or frequency yet, but clearly documented emerging risks: declining response rates, an undetermined disclosure-avoidance mandate, and demonstrated willingness to strip items from the closely related annual pension survey.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue (elements present):**
- Statutory authorization is explicitly named and longstanding: Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 161 and 182 are cited on the ICR, the questionnaire, and program pages — authorization is not vague.
- Strong, documented programmatic use: the Federal Reserve Board is the primary user (quarterly Flow of Funds/Financial Accounts, Table L.120.b), and BEA uses QSPP as a primary source for the government sector of the NIPA/GDP accounts. The ICR abstract explicitly states the FRB "uses these data to track the public sector portion of the Flow of Funds Accounts."

**Evidence for High Risk (elements present):**
- The rubric counts "alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes" toward High Risk. Partial substitutes exist: the Annual Survey of Public Pensions (F-11) collects the same financial content annually at state and system level, and the Census of Governments benchmarks the universe quinquennially. The Census Bureau demonstrated in April 2025 that it will cancel surveys when it claims "reliable alternatives" exist (the canceled 2026 local-government classification survey).

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- QSPP is not statutorily *required*; participation is voluntary (13 U.S.C. § 182 "voluntary assistance"), and no statute mandates quarterly pension publication.
- But for the survey's core purpose — quarterly asset-composition data for the Fed's Financial Accounts and BEA's national accounts — **no quarterly substitute exists**; the alternatives are annual or quinquennial and cannot serve the flow-of-funds use case. That is precisely why the Fed and CEA requested the survey in 1968.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** Explicit statutory authorization and indispensable programmatic use prevent the High Risk reading in spirit, but the collection is discretionary (not mandated), and annual-frequency partial substitutes exist — which bars "No Known Issue." (If one treats the Annual Survey of Public Pensions as a full substitute, this category would flip to High Risk.)

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Staff:** The Census Bureau lost an estimated **15% of its staff since FY24** (AMSTAT, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025"; AP News). Rep. Grace Meng publicly cited "the loss of over 1,000 Census Bureau staff" as of mid-2025 (Census Project, June 2025). The 43-day October 2025 shutdown furloughed most Bureau staff and generated ~100 RIF notices (temporarily rescinded by court order) plus ~300 Commerce-wide layoffs (Bloomberg Government via Census Project, Oct. 2025). The rubric's High Risk threshold — "1,000 or more staff lost" — is met at the agency level.
- **Leadership:** AMSTAT documents significant "leadership instability" and "leadership gaps" at the Bureau in 2025–2026; the Bureau has been led by an *acting* director (referenced as such in mid-2026 official communications), and the FY26 President's Budget proposed reorganizing BLS, BEA, and Census under Commerce. "Leadership removed" is another rubric High Risk trigger.

**Evidence against High Risk (context):**
- Budget: FY2026 enacted funding was **$1.490 billion, a $108 million increase** over FY24/FY25 (P.L. 119-74; CRS IF13105) — no top-line cut. However, the Current Surveys and Programs account (home of current economic statistics like QSPP) declined from $329M to **$319M (~3%)**, and the Administration's request ($289M, a 12.3% cut targeting programs like SIPP) signals intent even though Congress restored most of it.
- QSPP itself is a tiny program (~$449K/year; 400 responses; 300 burden hours per the ICR) that has continued operating without interruption through releases 2025–2026, suggesting program-level resilience within a weakened bureau.

**Verdict: High Risk.** Measured at the agency level required by the rubric, the Bureau has exceeded the 1,000-staff-loss threshold (~15% loss, >1,000 employees), has lost stable Senate-confirmed leadership, and has absorbed hiring freezes and shutdown furloughs. The relevant appropriations account was cut ~3%. The QSPP program has so far been spared direct effects, but the producing organization is substantially weakened.

## Policy

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Nothing has changed *what QSPP collects or publishes*: the December 2024 ICR renewal was an "extension without change," all 2026 releases came out on the normal schedule, and there is no negative policy note on the QSPP program pages.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- The **June 4, 2026 Commerce Department Administrative Order 216-26** is an administration-driven directive covering "all statistical products disseminated by the Census Bureau," banning noise infusion in favor of coarsening/suppression. It has already indefinitely delayed the 2025 ACS one-year data release and "has upended planning for Census 2030" (NPR, June 2026; Census Project, June 2026; NC OSBM, Sept. 2026). Scientific societies (APDU, COPAFS, PAA) formally protested it. If read as "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities," this would trigger High Risk — though its mechanism (disclosure avoidance for confidential microdata) has little practical purchase on QSPP's public-record national aggregates.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The administration has a clear, repeated pattern of terminating or restructuring statistical collections on burden/cost grounds: cancellation of the 2026 local-government classification survey (April 2025), the proposed SIPP "transformation" to a smaller sample with administrative data, delayed HTOPS collections, and the **August 2026 proposal to restructure the Annual Survey of Public Pensions and drop sixteen actuarial items** — the closest policy action yet to QSPP, in its own program family.
- None of these, however, has been directed at QSPP, whose small burden and Fed/BEA customer base give it a strong constituency.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** QSPP itself is untouched, but pending, undetermined policy (DAO 216-26 implementation) plus demonstrated administration-priority-driven changes to adjacent and sibling surveys fit "proposed or pending changes" rather than completed, QSPP-specific changes. This is the category I would most expect to escalate if DAO 216-26 implementation sweeps in economic products, or if the next ICR cycle (due before 12/31/2027) proposes "burden reduction" changes to Form F-10.

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
— All 1968–present data remain fully accessible on Census, API, and FRED/ALFRED with no alterations.

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
— Q3 2025 release slipped ~3–4 weeks to Jan. 15, 2026 due to the government shutdown; releases otherwise on schedule; ICR active through 12/31/2027.

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk**
— Format unchanged, but unit response rates fell from 96–99% (2024) to 76% (Q1 2026), increasing imputation; DAO 216-26 and sibling-survey item cuts pose emerging threats.

**Statutory Context: Moderate Risk**
— Explicit authorization (13 U.S.C. §§ 161, 182) and indispensable Fed/BEA programmatic use, but the collection is voluntary and not statutorily mandated, with annual-frequency partial substitutes in the same program family.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk**
— Census Bureau lost ~15% of staff (>1,000 employees), is under an acting director, endured shutdown furloughs/RIFs, and saw its Current Surveys account cut ~3% — meeting rubric High Risk thresholds even though QSPP-specific operations continue.

**Policy: Moderate Risk**
— No QSPP-specific change yet (ICR renewed "without change"), but the June 2026 disclosure-avoidance order, the canceled 2025 local-government survey, and the proposed gutting of actuarial items in the annual pension survey signal a clear administration direction that could reach QSPP at the next ICR renewal.

**Overall read:** QSPP is a small, cheap, well-institutionalized survey with powerful federal customers (Fed, BEA), which has so far weathered a severely disrupted operating environment at its parent agency — the most likely failure modes are not outright termination but quiet degradation: further response-rate erosion, delayed releases during future shutdowns, and burden-reduction edits at the 2027 ICR renewal.
